content: Malaria is a vector-borne infectious disease caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium. It is one of the most prevalent infectious diseases globally and represents a significant public health challenge. The most severe forms of malaria are caused by Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, although other species such as Plasmodium ovale, Plasmodium malariae, and occasionally Plasmodium knowlesi can also infect humans. Collectively, these species are referred to as malaria parasites. Malaria is one of the oldest known infections in human history. Initially, its symptoms were thought to be caused by harmful environmental elements. In 1880, Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran discovered the Plasmodium parasite in blood smears of malaria patients. The role of mosquitoes in transmitting malaria to humans was identified a few years later. However, the complete life cycle of the Plasmodium parasite remained unclear until 1982. Historically, malaria has been treated with quinine, an alkaloid derived from the bark of cinchona trees. The first synthetic quinine was produced in 1948. In 2014, the first candidate for an anti-malarial vaccine was developed. In humans, malaria progresses through two distinct phases: the exoerythrocytic (hepatic) phase and the erythrocytic phase. When an infected mosquito bites a person, sporozoites in the mosquito's saliva enter the bloodstream and migrate to the liver. Malaria can be classified based on the species of Plasmodium involved. Five species commonly infect humans: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi. It can also be categorized by the severity of the infection, as either uncomplicated or severe. Malaria is caused by protozoan parasites transmitted through the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. P. vivax is the most common cause of infection, accounting for approximately 80% of all malaria cases. However, P. falciparum is the most clinically significant species, responsible for about 15% of infections and 90% of malaria-related deaths. Approximately 4 billion people live in areas at risk of malaria transmission across 106 countries and territories. In 2012, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that malaria caused 207 million clinical episodes and 627,000 deaths, with 91% of deaths in 2010 occurring in the African region. The majority of malaria cases occur in children under the age of five. Malaria is endemic in regions around the equator, including parts of the Americas, Asia, and Africa, with sub-Saharan Africa accounting for 85–90% of malaria fatalities. The distribution of malaria is influenced by climatic factors such as temperature, humidity, and rainfall. Travel to endemic areas is a significant risk factor for malaria. Regions with the highest relative risk of infection for travelers include West Africa and Oceania. Socioeconomic factors and human behavior can also influence malaria risk. Children and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to malaria. Certain genetic traits, such as the sickle cell trait and the absence of the Duffy blood group, provide some protection against specific types of malaria. Screening for malaria is essential in populations such as sub-Saharan refugees and blood donors. After the bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito, there is an incubation period before symptoms appear. This period ranges from 7 to 30 days, depending on factors such as the patient’s immune status, the Plasmodium species and strain, the dose of sporozoites transmitted, and the use of prophylactic drugs. A classical malaria attack, though rarely observed, lasts 6–10 hours and consists of three stages: a cold stage, a hot stage, and a sweating stage. Severe malaria, almost exclusively caused by P. falciparum, typically develops 6–14 days after infection. Complications of severe malaria include splenomegaly, severe headache, cerebral ischemia, hepatomegaly, hypotension, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and hemoglobinuria with renal failure. Severe malaria can progress rapidly and lead to death within hours or days. In the most severe cases, fatality rates can exceed 20%, even with intensive care and treatment. The hallmark symptom of malaria is fever, often occurring in paroxysms separated by fever-free intervals. A classical malaria attack, though rare, lasts 6–10 hours and includes a cold stage, a hot stage, and a sweating stage. Other common symptoms include chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, night sweats, flu-like symptoms, and myalgia. A history of travel to a malaria-endemic region is a critical diagnostic clue in the presence of paroxysmal fever. It is essential to distinguish between uncomplicated and severe malaria, as the latter is a medical emergency that can cause organ damage. Physical examination findings in malaria may include fever, weakness, pallor, jaundice, and perspiration. Additional findings may include tachycardia, tachypnea, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly. The diagnosis of malaria is confirmed by identifying the malaria parasite in the patient’s blood under microscopy. Laboratory tests may reveal anemia with decreased hemoglobin, hematocrit, and haptoglobin, as well as either a decreased or increased leukocyte count. Biochemical findings may include hypoglycemia, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), acidosis, and mild hyponatremia due to vomiting and diarrhea. In severe cases, elevated creatinine, proteinuria, and hemoglobinuria may indicate renal failure. Malaria-specific diagnostic tests include antigen detection tests, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and serology for Plasmodium-specific antibodies. Drug resistance testing is also recommended to assess the susceptibility of the parasite to antimalarial drugs. Imaging studies such as X-rays, ultrasound, CT scans, and MRI are not required for the diagnosis of malaria. However, ultrasound may be used to assess splenomegaly or complications of malaria. Active malaria infection with P. falciparum is a medical emergency requiring hospitalization. Infections with P. vivax, P. ovale, or P. malariae can often be treated on an outpatient basis. Treatment involves supportive measures and specific antimalarial drugs. With proper treatment, malaria is curable. Currently, no vaccine is widely available for malaria, although several are under development. The RTS,S malaria vaccine was proposed in July 2014 and is pending approval by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). Another vaccine, the PfSPZ malaria vaccine, is being studied for clinical efficacy. Preventative drugs must be taken continuously to reduce the risk of infection. Adults from endemic areas often develop partial resistance to malaria, but this resistance diminishes over time if they move to non-endemic regions. Individuals returning to endemic areas are strongly advised to take full precautions. Malaria transmission can be reduced by preventing mosquito bites through the use of mosquito nets, insect repellents, and mosquito control measures such as indoor insecticide spraying and draining standing water where mosquitoes breed. Although effective antimalarial drugs are available, access to these drugs remains a challenge for people in endemic areas due to cost and limited availability of healthcare facilities. The RTS,S vaccine is considered the first candidate for an antimalarial vaccine. Phase 3 trials in young African children have demonstrated significant efficacy beyond conventional preventative measures. If approved, the World Health Organization (WHO) plans to recommend the RTS,S vaccine. Other vaccines are also in development but require further validation of their clinical efficacy.
